title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study comparing a baseline single‑shot LLM configuration generator against a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline (with a canary stage) on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus (2000 paired episodes). The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) and validation used a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; downstream validation and the permitted single repair call (guarded arm only) were the only mechanisms for paired outcome differences. Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference = 0.005 (n11=995, n10=5, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). The preregistered secondary descriptive summary (paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.001, 0.01]. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred and total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). We present the exact McNemar result as the preregistered confirmatory outcome, present the bootstrap CI as a secondary descriptive summary, explicitly label a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) as exploratory/post‑hoc, and interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in light of sparse discordant counts, high baseline validity, validator scope, and the shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation for network operations promises reduced manual effort but raises safety risks: multi‑step sequencing errors, transient invariant violations, and protected‑field interference can convert plausible command sequences into harmful actions. Prior surveys and controlled studies document LLM hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that affect code and configuration generation, motivating architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair procedures [1], [2].

This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment (cand‑003‑stud‑001) that isolates purely downstream validator/repair effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Our precise research question is: when baseline and guarded conditions begin from the exact same sampled initial candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics), to what degree can a downstream deterministic validator plus a single allowed repair call (guarded pipeline with a canary stage) improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes compared with reusing the same initial candidate unmodified (baseline)? The design intentionally isolates downstream interventions (validation and at‑most‑one repair) so that any paired difference is attributable to those downstream mechanisms rather than to first‑pass generation differences such as prompt engineering, constrained decoding, or sampling variance.

Contributions. (i) A preregistered paired experiment (Npairs = 1000) with deterministic task selection from the challenging_workflow_stress_v1 corpus and archived validator traces. (ii) Full execution accounting and artifact publication (completed pairs = 1000; hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005; repair calls = 5; model declared = gpt‑5‑mini; model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset — null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). (iii) Transparent reporting that the preregistered primary test (exact two‑sided McNemar) did not reach two‑sided α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625), accompanied by preregistered descriptive summaries (paired bootstrap CI = [0.001, 0.01], seed = 1729) and explicit labeling of any post‑hoc directional tests as exploratory.
sections.related_work:
LLM failures in structured outputs. Empirical surveys and controlled experiments document hallucinations and prompt sensitivity that materially affect correctness of generated code and configuration artifacts [2], and several NetOps‑focused works demonstrate LLMs can produce plausible but unsafe configuration sequences absent verifier checks [4].

Generate→validate→repair and constrained decoding. Prior work advocates pairing generation with deterministic validators, schema constraints, or constrained decoding to increase executable/valid output rates in structured domains; most demonstrations show gains in executability but vary in effect size and domain transfer [3]. Recent NetOps and agentic‑AI system papers emphasize verifier‑assisted repair, governance/protocol enforcement, and auditability (proof‑carrying proposals) as mitigations for automation risks, arguing operational reliability depends on validator coverage and external governance rather than on any single model [5], [6], [7].

Positioning. Our experiment differs from prior evaluations by preregistering a paired design under shared_initial_candidate semantics that holds the initial sampled candidate constant across arms; this isolates the incremental effect of downstream deterministic validation and a bounded repair budget, rather than conflating downstream safeguards with independent first‑pass generation or prompting interventions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design freeze. The experiment preregistration (cand‑003‑stud‑001) was finalized prior to any hosted‑model invocation; its preregistration SHA‑256 is recorded in the execution manifest (ab4c6436c6ece56bf47da7730d50485a17cdb9bb86a90a4231042303d3b489ec). Key preregistered elements: paired confirmatory binary design; task_count = 1000 deterministic tasks drawn from the challenging_workflow_stress_v1 synthetic corpus; generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (exactly one sampled initial generation per pair deterministically reused by both conditions); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact two‑sided McNemar. Secondary preregistered summaries include a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) and sensitivity analyses treating failed calls as unsafe.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and causal interpretation. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics both baseline and guarded episodes begin from the same sampled candidate; the guarded pipeline may invoke the single allowed repair call but no independent first‑pass generation is performed for the guarded arm. Consequently, any paired outcome difference can only arise from deterministic validator decisions and permitted repair(s). This design deliberately isolates downstream safeguards and therefore does not estimate effects attributable to alternative prompting or to independent constrained‑decoding generations.

Models, validator, and runtime caveats. Declared model/provider: gpt‑5‑mini (provider = openai_responses); orchestration adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; validator/digital twin = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The validator enforces manifest workflow policies (required command presence and order, protected‑field noninterference) and returns a deterministic binary safe‑deploy verdict per episode.

Task corpus and selection. Tasks are synthetic and difficult (labels: very_hard, extreme) and include detailed initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, and allowed_touched_fields. The deterministic selection rule produced 1000 unique task indices as preregistered. The validator compares parsed candidate command sequences against task manifests in a deterministic digital‑twin emulator and emits structured traces stored per episode.

Execution controls and missingness. Retries were limited by preregistration (maximum_attempts_per_call = 1). The execution manifest documents completed_episode_count = 2000, failed_episode_count = 0, hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005, stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation = 1000, repair = 5}; the analysis executor applied the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' missingness treatment and preregistered sensitivity analyses were available in the archive.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and artifacts. The run executed the full preregistered plan: planned episodes = 2000, completed = 2000, complete_pairs = 1000, failed episodes = 0. Provider audit (deterministic_reconciliation.json) records hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5) and no cross‑condition cache reuse. All deterministic consistency checks passed; contamination checks and exclusion rules registered no prompt‑leakage flags.

Paired outcomes and preregistered primary test. The observed contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 995 (both success), n10 = 5 (guarded success, baseline failure), n01 = 0 (baseline success, guarded failure), n00 = 0 (both failure). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The preregistered confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) returns p = 0.0625; this does not meet the preregistered two‑sided α = 0.05, so H1 is not supported under the prespecified confirmatory analysis.

Preregistered descriptive summaries and exploratory tests. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) yields [0.001, 0.01]; this descriptive CI excludes zero because bootstrap percentile intervals can be sensitive to extremely sparse discordant counts. A one‑sided McNemar (guarded > baseline) yields p = 0.03125; because a directional one‑sided test was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration it is explicitly reported as exploratory/post‑hoc and does not alter the preregistered confirmatory conclusion.

Repair traces. Five validator‑triggered repairs occurred (repair stage_count = 5). Representative episode artifacts demonstrate the validator rejecting initial candidates for violations (e.g., required_sequence ordering or protected‑field touches), the adapter invoking the single permitted repair call, and the validator accepting the repaired candidate on revalidation. All raw responses, provider call traces, repair traces, and validator traces are archived for inspection (execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json).
sections.discussion:
Inferential hierarchy and interpretation. The preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar is the primary confirmatory analysis and it did not reach two‑sided α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap CI ([0.001, 0.01]) is a preregistered descriptive summary sensitive to sparse discordant counts; the one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) is explicitly exploratory because it was not prespecified. These statements together form the preregistered inferential hierarchy and should guide interpretation.

Power assumptions and sensitivity. The preregistered power plan assumed baseline ≈ 0.60 and targeted an absolute effect of 0.15; the observed baseline (0.995) is far higher, producing very few discordant pairs and substantially reducing sensitivity of the prespecified exact paired test to detect small absolute gains. This baseline–power mismatch explains why a small absolute observed improvement (0.005) does not reach prespecified two‑sided significance even though the bootstrap CI excludes zero under resampling.

Mechanistic implications within shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because both arms began from the same sampled candidate, paired differences can only arise from validation decisions and permitted repairs. The five observed repairs confirm that deterministic validators with adequate rule coverage can correct some sequence/constraint violations; however, low repair incidence limits inference about repair efficacy across failure modes. Measuring generation‑level interventions (e.g., constrained decoding, prompt templates) requires independent first‑pass generation arms not executed here.

Threats to validity and external generalizability. Construct validity depends on validator rule coverage: omitted semantic checks would inflate success rates. External validity is limited by a single model (gpt‑5‑mini) and a synthetic task corpus; production heterogeneity (vendor devices, legacy stacks) is not represented. Conclusion validity is constrained by sparse discordant counts reducing test power; these limitations are documented in the archived evidence and the manuscript's Limitations section.

Operational implications and recommended follow‑ups. Artifact‑grounded evidence shows downstream verifier‑guided repair can avert certain unsafe outcomes in synthetic workflows, but measurable marginal gains depend on baseline failure prevalence, validator coverage, and repair budget. Preregistered follow‑ups supported by the archive include: (i) independent first‑pass generation arms to measure prompt/decoding effects, (ii) repair‑budget sweeps to quantify marginal returns per failure class, (iii) expanded validator rule suites and topology heterogeneity, and (iv) multi‑model evaluations. Each follow‑up should be preregistered with power calculations aligned to plausible baseline failure rates.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study under shared_initial_candidate semantics on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline generated a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) relative to a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test did not reach α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs were invoked and total model calls used = 1005. The preregistered confirmatory McNemar result is the primary inferential conclusion; directional tests reported post‑hoc are exploratory and do not change the preregistered outcome. These artifact‑grounded results indicate downstream verifier/repair safeguards can prevent some unsafe outcomes, but measurable marginal gains are constrained when baseline outputs are already highly valid and when the paired design isolates downstream effects. Full preregistration, execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived with the run to support reproducibility and preregistered follow‑ups that broaden model diversity, validator coverage, and repair budgets.

limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch is reported explicitly and reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
